findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the cleanup function
findings.body: When a caller invokes the returned disposer, the `"message"` handler remains active. This breaks the cleanup contract and causes disposed handlers to receive later messages; repeated attach/cleanup cycles also retain listeners and duplicate processing.

findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup function
findings.body:
After any caller invokes the returned teardown function, subsequent `"message"` events still invoke `handler`. Repeated attach/cleanup cycles also accumulate listeners, causing duplicate processing and memory leaks. This universally breaks the existing cancellation contract.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup function
findings.body:
Any caller invoking the returned disposer expects the registered `"message"` handler to be detached. The no-op leaves it active, so later messages still invoke disposed handlers and repeated attach/cleanup cycles accumulate duplicate listeners.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal during teardown
findings.body:
The returned cleanup function no longer unregisters the handler. If consumers invoke it during logout, authorization revocation, or socket reuse, an attacker who can continue sending messages can still trigger the expired handler, potentially causing unauthorized actions or cross-session message exposure.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
